analysis.one_liner: Required large employers to offer workers affordable family health coverage.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2002 with one cosponsor, sent to the Senate health committee, and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Health Care for Working Families Act would have used the same federal law that sets the minimum wage to make large employers provide health benefits. Any company with 100 or more employees would have to offer a family health plan as good as the one federal workers get, and pay at least 75% of the premium, with the worker's share taken out of pay. Part-time workers would get a prorated employer contribution, and contract, temporary, and leased workers would count as employees. The bill also applied to contractors that do most of their work for a single large employer, so companies could not dodge the requirement by outsourcing.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at companies with 100 or more employees who lack family health coverage, plus their spouses and children — the bill's findings note that most uninsured Americans are workers or their dependents. It also reaches part-time workers (10–30 hours a week, with a scaled-down employer contribution) and contract, temporary, and leased workers who today often get no benefits at all.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and families lacking employer health coverage

how_it_helps.text: Every employer with 100 or more employees would have to offer workers a health plan covering the whole family, with benefits at least as good as the Blue Cross/Blue Shield Standard Plan available to federal employees as of January 1, 2002.

The employer would have to pay at least 75% of the premium; for part-time workers, the required contribution scales with hours (for example, 15 hours a week earns half the standard contribution), and workers under 10 hours a week are excluded.
Coverage would have to start within 30 days of an employee's first hour of work, so new hires would not face waiting periods.
Contract, temporary, and leased workers count as employees of the company they work for, closing a common route employers used to avoid providing benefits.
Subcontractors that do most of their work for a single large employer are covered too, so companies could not escape the mandate by outsourcing their workforce.

analysis.who_pays: Large employers — companies with 100 or more employees — which would bear at least 75% of family-plan premiums for full-time workers and prorated shares for part-timers, enforced by civil money penalties and injunctions under existing labor-law procedures. Workers would pay up to 25% of the premium through payroll withholding.

drawbacks.text: The mandate applies only to employers with 100 or more employees, so the millions of uninsured people working for small businesses would get no help from this bill.
Workers would still pay up to 25% of the family premium out of their own wages, which for a low-wage employee could be a meaningful expense even with the employer subsidy.

Requiring every large employer to pay at least 75% of a family-coverage premium is a substantial new payroll cost; the bill offered no offsetting tax relief or funding, so some of the cost would likely surface as slower hiring, lower raises, or higher prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit was real: family health coverage for millions of workers who today get none, at a standard of benefits equal to what federal employees receive. The costs were also real: a large new payroll obligation for big employers, likely some mix of lower wages, slower hiring, or higher prices, and premium shares of up to 25% that could still strain low-wage family budgets. The bill was deliberately narrow (100+ employees), which contained the cost but left out most small businesses and their uninsured workers. It was a broad step toward universal coverage for one large slice of the workforce, but not universal coverage.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate health committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died there when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Senator Kennedy introduced S. 2639 on June 18, 2002, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
That referral was the last action of any kind on the bill; it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or consideration on the Senate floor.
The bill died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, having received only one roll of action: introduction and committee referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large employers, particularly those that would have had to start paying 75% of family premiums, were better off because the bill never advanced. Workers without employer family coverage gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large employers that would have paid the premiums

for.name: Edward M. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 18, 2002 and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Jon Corzine
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, the only cosponsor it received.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 18, 2002 and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress — no hearing, no markup, no report.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of the Senate as a whole was never tested; both sponsors were Democrats, and no Republican or other Democrat signed on.

industries.industry: Large employers (100+ employees), especially those that do not currently offer family coverage
industries.note: These companies would have to offer family coverage and pay at least 75% of the premium for full-time workers, with prorated contributions for part-timers. The bill's own findings concede that most large employers already provide this, so the direct cost falls hardest on the minority that do not.

Every covered employer would have to buy a private plan meeting the federal benefit standard, and insurers would be required to sell compliant coverage. Insurers gain a large pool of mandated customers at the same time workers gain coverage, so their interest runs alongside the public's here.

Their workers would count as employees entitled to coverage, but the bill lets a staffing firm satisfy the requirement by providing compliant coverage itself, so the burden is softened rather than eliminated.
